identity.title: Learning Linear Attention in Polynomial Time

problem.claim: Determine whether single-layer Transformers with linear attention can be efficiently learned from data.

gap.claim: Prior work addressed Transformer expressivity, but efficient learnability from data remained open.

contributions.claim: Provides polynomial-time strong, agnostic PAC learning results for single-layer linear-attention Transformers.
Recasts optimal multi-head linear-attention learning as optimal kernel prediction in a suitably defined RKHS.
Constructs a polynomial-time dataset check for whether all best-fit multi-head networks compute identically, proposed as a notion relevant to out-of-distribution generalization.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors characterize their results as the first polynomial-time learnability results of this type for single-layer Transformers with linear attention.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report empirical validation on learning random linear-attention networks, key–value associations, and executing finite automata.
The authors report a polynomial-time test for identical computation among all best-fit networks on a dataset.

narrative_sequence.summary: Prior research studied Transformer expressivity through Boolean-circuit and Turing-machine simulation.
Efficient learning of Transformers from data is identified as unresolved.
The study introduces polynomial-time strong, agnostic PAC learnability results for single-layer linear attention and connects optimal learning to RKHS prediction.
It proposes a polynomial-time identical-computation check for best-fit networks and reports validation on three canonical task families.
The authors frame the findings as bridging Transformer expressivity and learnability.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links an attention-learning problem to optimal kernel prediction in a suitably defined RKHS.

lessons.interpretation: A representation change can make the computational structure of a learning problem more tractable and expose applicable theory.
lessons.application: When presenting a theoretical learning result, explicitly identify an equivalent optimization or prediction formulation and state what it enables computationally.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the equivalence is only heuristic or does not preserve the target objective.

source_observation.claim: Given a dataset, the abstract describes a polynomial-time check of whether all best-fit multi-head linear-attention networks perform an identical computation, and connects this property to out-of-distribution generalization.

lessons.interpretation: Generalization claims can be sharpened by defining a concrete, testable property of the solution set.
lessons.application: For models with multiple empirical optima, define and analyze a solution-set property that is computable from observed data before making broader generalization claims.
lessons.exception: This approach may be unsuitable when the relevant model class is misspecified or when its best-fit solution set cannot be characterized by a tractable check.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the precise model assumptions, RKHS construction, dataset conditions, or polynomial-time complexity bounds.
The empirical abstract does not report metrics, baselines, dataset sizes, or quantitative results.

editorial_revisions.before: The abstract separates fitting behavior from a polynomial-time check that all best-fit models compute identically on the dataset, connecting this property to out-of-distribution generalization.
editorial_revisions.after: Given a dataset, the abstract describes a polynomial-time check of whether all best-fit multi-head linear-attention networks perform an identical computation, and connects this property to out-of-distribution generalization.
